opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, a lot of it comes down to leverage. When you have one architecture, or a very small number of them, every improvement compounds. If someone on the team figures out a better way to stabilize training, a better optimizer setting, or a better way to scale context, that win shows up everywhere at once: in the image model, the audio model, the text model. If you've fragmented into five bespoke stacks, each insight has to be re-derived and re-implemented five times, and in practice a lot of them just never make it across.

There's also a scientific reason. Some of the most interesting things happen when modalities share a representation. A model that sees text and images in the same space can transfer what it learns in one to the other. You get reasoning that grounds in vision, and visual understanding that benefits from all the world knowledge in language. That transfer is much harder to get if you've architected the modalities apart from the start.

Then there's the infrastructure side, which people underrate. Every distinct architecture means its own kernels, its own inference path, its own evals and debugging tools. That's a real tax on a research org. Consolidating means your infrastructure people can go really deep on making one thing fast and reliable instead of spreading themselves thin.

None of this means you never specialize. Sometimes a modality really does need something different, like how you tokenize audio or handle the spatial structure of video. But the default posture I like is: start from the shared backbone, and make anyone who wants to deviate justify it with results. That keeps the lab moving as one research program rather than a collection of separate ones.

r001.rationale: It says each distinct architecture requires its own kernels, inference path, evaluations, and debugging tools, creating a tax on the research organization.

r002.rationale: It says improvements to training, optimization, and context scaling on a shared architecture can benefit image, audio, and text models, and describes learning transferring across modalities.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer this one directly as the guest, no tools needed.

Yeah, so the honest answer is that it's partly a bet about where the intelligence comes from and partly a bet about how you run a lab.

On the first part: every time we've tried to maintain a bespoke stack for one modality, we end up relearning the same lessons in parallel. You figure something out about data mixing or scaling behavior or how to stabilize training on the language side, and then six months later someone on the image side rediscovers it from scratch with a slightly different vocabulary. That's just waste. If the core architecture is shared, an improvement to the transformer backbone, or to the optimizer, or to how you tokenize and interleave data, lands everywhere at once. You get compounding instead of a bunch of separate little hills being climbed.

The deeper reason, though, is that I don't actually think these are different problems. A video is a sequence. Audio is a sequence. Text is a sequence. Images you can treat as a sequence if you're willing to. The thing that made language models work was not some clever language-specific trick, it was a generic sequence model plus a lot of data plus scale. So the prior should be that the same recipe works for everything else, and the burden of proof is on the person who wants to add a special-case architecture. Sometimes that proof exists, and we've had moments where a diffusion-style approach or a specialized encoder genuinely won on quality for a while. But I treat those as temporary. The question I always ask is: is this a fundamental advantage, or is it that we haven't scaled the unified thing enough yet? Historically the answer has mostly been the second one.

And then there's the organizational piece, which people underrate. A lab is a finite number of very good researchers and a finite amount of compute. If you have five architectures, you have five infra stacks, five sets of eval harnesses, five groups that each think their problem is the special one. Nobody can move between projects without a learning curve. Consolidating down to one or two means a researcher who's been doing audio can go help on video next month and actually be productive. It also makes the compute conversation much simpler, because you're not arbitrating between five teams who each want their own big run.

The last thing I'd say is that the end state we actually care about is a single model that can see, hear, read, and produce all of those. You can't get there by stapling together five models at the end. The interfaces between them become the bottleneck and the model never learns the cross-modal stuff that makes it interesting, like reasoning about what's happening in a video while someone is talking over it. So keeping everything close architecturally from the beginning isn't just efficient, it's kind of the only path to the thing we're trying to build.

r001.rationale: The response says that five architectures require five infrastructure stacks and eval harnesses, and that consolidating architectures reduces this burden.

r002.rationale: It explains that improvements to a shared backbone, optimizer, or data approach can benefit every modality, and that researchers otherwise rediscover the same lessons in parallel.

astra-6.text:
For me, a lot of it comes down to research leverage. If image, audio, video, and text all require completely different architectures, you end up with separate stacks and separate sets of tricks. An improvement in one area doesn’t necessarily help the others, and it becomes harder for researchers to move between them.

If you can share the underlying architecture, an improvement to the way you train or scale the model can benefit several modalities at once. You can also start asking whether learning from one modality helps with another. Video has information about how the world changes that’s hard to capture in text alone; audio carries information that a transcript loses.

That doesn’t mean you should force everything into exactly the same representation. There are real differences between modalities. But I like having as much shared machinery as possible, so the research compounds and you have fewer independent problems to solve.

r001.rationale: It mentions separate stacks and fewer independent problems, but does not clearly identify their infrastructure maintenance cost.

r002.rationale: It says improvements to training or scaling a shared architecture can benefit several modalities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest reason is that you want research progress to compound. If your image team discovers something that makes training more stable or improves the architecture, you want the audio and video teams to benefit from that without having to reinvent it for their own stack. If every modality has a completely different architecture, sharing those improvements becomes much harder.

There’s also a lot of structure shared across modalities. A video has images, sound, and often language, and you’d like the model to learn those relationships together. Keeping the architectures similar makes it easier to bring those capabilities into one model.

That doesn’t mean forcing everything to be identical. Some modality-specific pieces may make sense. But I’d rather start with a shared approach and introduce differences when the research shows we need them.

r001.rationale: The response says separate architectures make it harder to share improvements, but does not identify infrastructure maintenance cost as a reason to minimize architectural diversity.

r002.rationale: It says research improvements in one modality, such as training stability or architecture, can benefit the audio and video teams without being reinvented.
